stem: Which of the following is a purpose of a test plan?
options: It records every defect found during test execution, with its current status
It proves that the test object meets all of its requirements
It holds the detailed steps and expected results of each test case
It documents the means and the schedule for achieving the test objectives
why: A test plan documents how (means) and when (schedule) the test objectives will be reached; it is also a communication tool and shows how testing follows the test policy and strategy.

distractorNotes.A: Defects and their status are tracked in defect reports and the defect management tool, not in the test plan.
distractorNotes.B: Overgeneralisation: no test document proves that; a plan describes how testing will be done.
distractorNotes.C: Steps and expected results are testware from test design and implementation (test cases, test procedures), not the plan.

stem: You are writing the test plan for a racing game's online season update. Which item belongs in the plan's risk register?
options: The test cases for the new lap-timer feature, with their expected results
The defect report for the pit-stop crash found in last week's build
The requirements coverage achieved at the end of system testing
The licensed car models may arrive late from the manufacturer, and races may desync with more than 12 players
why: The risk register in a test plan lists both project risks (a late supplier delivery) and product risks (desync under load).

distractorNotes.A: Test cases are designed later in test design; they are not risks.
distractorNotes.B: A defect that has already been found is not a risk; it lives in defect management.
distractorNotes.C: Achieved coverage is a result for a progress or completion report, not a risk.

stem: Which of the following belongs to the test approach section of a test plan?
options: The test levels, test techniques and entry and exit criteria to be used
The stakeholders' roles, responsibilities and training needs
The budget and the schedule of the test project
The lessons learned from the finished test project
why: The test approach covers test levels, test types, test techniques, test deliverables, entry and exit criteria, independence, metrics, test data and environment requirements, and deviations from organisational practice.

distractorNotes.B: Category smear: this is in the test plan, but in the stakeholders section, not the test approach.
distractorNotes.C: Category smear: budget and schedule are their own part of the test plan.
distractorNotes.D: Lessons learned belong to the test completion report, written at the end.

stem: After the test plan for a city-builder's console port is approved, the producer says: "Now it is signed, nobody changes it until release." Which statement about test plans is CORRECT?
options: A test plan can only be written once all requirements are frozen
In iterative development there is no test plan; the product backlog replaces it
A test plan is updated as the project progresses and feedback becomes available
Changes to the plan are recorded only in the test completion report
why: Planning is continuous: the plan is refined as more is learned, risks change and feedback arrives.

distractorNotes.A: Planning starts early, before everything is known; that is why the plan is updated later.
distractorNotes.B: Iterative teams still plan testing (release and iteration planning, test plans at different levels).
distractorNotes.D: The completion report notes deviations from the plan at the end; the plan itself is updated during the project.

stem: While planning the testing of a VR rhythm game, the test manager notices that nobody on the team has a headset yet and that the publisher's certification slot is in six weeks. Which benefit of test planning does this show?
options: Planning removes the need for test monitoring and control later in the project
Planning guarantees that the game will pass certification
Planning replaces the organisation's test strategy for this project
Planning makes the team face future challenges, such as risks, schedules, people and tools, before they happen
why: Writing the plan forces thinking ahead about risks, schedules, people, tools, costs and effort, so problems like missing hardware show up early.

distractorNotes.A: Planning does not replace monitoring and control; the plan is the baseline they compare against.
distractorNotes.B: Overgeneralisation: a plan cannot guarantee an outcome.
distractorNotes.C: The plan shows how testing follows (or deviates from) the test strategy; it does not replace it.

stem: Which information belongs in the "context of testing" part of a test plan?
options: The forms, frequency and templates of communication
The scope, test objectives, constraints and test basis
The test data and test environment requirements
The project risks and product risks
why: The context of testing describes scope, test objectives, constraints and the test basis.

distractorNotes.A: This is the communication part of the plan.
distractorNotes.C: These belong to the test approach.
distractorNotes.D: These belong to the risk register.

stem: Which statement about a test plan is CORRECT?
options: It defines the organisation's test policy for all future projects
It contains the actual results of each executed test case
It shows how testing will follow the test policy and test strategy, or explains why it deviates from them
It is only useful to the testers, so it is not shared with other stakeholders
why: One purpose of the test plan is to demonstrate that testing adheres to the existing test policy and strategy, or to explain the deviations.

distractorNotes.A: Adjacent-concept swap: the test policy is an organisation-level document; a test plan applies it to one project.
distractorNotes.B: Actual results are recorded in test logs and reports during execution.
distractorNotes.D: The plan is explicitly a means of communication with team members and other stakeholders.

stem: Which of the following is a way testers contribute to release planning?
options: Writing testable user stories and acceptance criteria
Breaking the stories of the current iteration down into testing tasks
Determining the testability of each user story in the iteration backlog
Fixing the defects reported in the previous release
why: In release planning testers write testable user stories and acceptance criteria, take part in risk analyses, estimate test effort, determine the test approach and plan the testing for the release.

distractorNotes.B: This is a contribution to iteration planning.
distractorNotes.C: This is a contribution to iteration planning (the iteration backlog).
distractorNotes.D: Wrong actor and wrong activity: fixing defects is development work, not a tester's planning contribution.

stem: Which of the following is a tester's contribution to iteration planning?
options: Defining and re-defining the product backlog for the release
Planning the testing for the whole release
Approving the release as the product owner
Breaking user stories down into tasks, particularly testing tasks
why: In iteration planning testers take part in the detailed risk analysis of stories, determine their testability, break them down into (testing) tasks, estimate the test effort for those tasks and refine functional and non-functional aspects.

distractorNotes.A: This is what release planning itself does.
distractorNotes.B: This is a contribution to release planning.
distractorNotes.C: Wrong actor: approval for release is not a tester's planning contribution.

stem: You are a tester on a team planning the next two-week sprint of a farming sim. Which activity is part of your contribution in this meeting?
options: Writing the test completion report for the sprint
Agreeing the release date with the publisher
Estimating the test effort for all the testing tasks of the sprint's stories
Splitting the year's large epics in the product backlog into smaller stories
why: Sprint planning is iteration planning: testers estimate the test effort for all the testing tasks of the iteration.

distractorNotes.A: A completion report is written at the end of the iteration, during test completion, not in planning.
distractorNotes.B: Not a tester contribution to iteration planning.
distractorNotes.D: Refining the product backlog for the release is release planning.

stem: Which pair correctly matches each planning horizon with what it is mainly concerned with?
options: Release planning: the iteration backlog. Iteration planning: the product backlog
Release planning: the product backlog. Iteration planning: the iteration backlog
Release planning: the test cases. Iteration planning: the test scripts
Release planning: the defect backlog. Iteration planning: the risk register
why: Release planning looks ahead to the release and works on the product backlog; iteration planning looks ahead to the end of one iteration and works on the iteration backlog.

distractorNotes.A: Swapped horizons.
distractorNotes.C: Test cases and scripts come from test design and implementation, not from the planning horizons.
distractorNotes.D: Neither horizon is defined by these work products.

stem: Which tester contribution is listed for BOTH release planning and iteration planning?
options: Determining the testability of user stories
Determining the test approach
Breaking user stories down into testing tasks
Estimating test effort
why: Testers estimate test effort in both: for the user stories in release planning, and for all testing tasks in iteration planning.

distractorNotes.A: Listed for iteration planning only.
distractorNotes.B: Listed for release planning only.
distractorNotes.C: Listed for iteration planning only.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a tester's contribution to iteration planning?
options: Planning the testing for the whole release
Identifying and refining the functional and non-functional aspects of the test object
Taking part in the detailed risk analysis of user stories
Determining the testability of user stories
why: Planning the testing for the release is a release planning contribution; the other three are iteration planning contributions.

distractorNotes.B: This IS an iteration planning contribution.
distractorNotes.C: This IS an iteration planning contribution.
distractorNotes.D: This IS an iteration planning contribution.

stem: Which of the following is a typical entry criterion?
options: Requirements coverage of 95% has been reached
All defects found have been reported
All smoke tests on the new build have passed
Fewer than five defects remain unresolved
why: The initial quality level of the test object (e.g. smoke tests passed) is a typical entry criterion.

distractorNotes.A: A measure of thoroughness: an exit criterion.
distractorNotes.B: A binary exit criterion.
distractorNotes.D: A measure of thoroughness: an exit criterion.

stem: Which of the following is a typical exit criterion?
options: The test environment and test data are available
Testable acceptance criteria exist for the story
The test team has the budget for this test level
All planned regression tests have been automated
why: Binary yes/no criteria such as "all regression tests are automated" are typical exit criteria.

distractorNotes.A: Availability of resources is an entry criterion.
distractorNotes.B: Availability of testware is an entry criterion.
distractorNotes.C: Availability of resources (budget) is an entry criterion.

stem: System testing of a puzzle game's level editor is due to start, but the editor build crashes on load and the level-format specification is still a draft. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: The exit criteria are not met, so system testing must be stopped
The entry criteria are not met, so starting now is likely to make testing harder, more costly and riskier
Entry criteria only apply to test levels that include formal reviews
The crash is an exit criterion for the next test level, so testing can start
why: Unmet entry criteria (no stable test object, no approved test basis) make the activity more difficult, time-consuming, costly and risky.

distractorNotes.A: Adjacent-concept swap: exit criteria are about finishing; this is about starting.
distractorNotes.C: Invented restriction: any activity or test level can have entry criteria.
distractorNotes.D: Confused: a crash on load is a quality level problem for starting this level.

stem: A test lead lists four criteria: 1. The test environment is available. 2. 80% branch coverage is reached. 3. The build has passed its smoke test. 4. No critical defects are open. Which classification is CORRECT?
options: 1 and 3 are entry criteria; 2 and 4 are exit criteria
1 and 2 are entry criteria; 3 and 4 are exit criteria
Only 1 is an entry criterion; 2, 3 and 4 are exit criteria
3 and 4 are entry criteria; 1 and 2 are exit criteria
why: Environment availability and an initial quality level (smoke test passed) are about starting; coverage reached and open defects are about finishing.

distractorNotes.B: Coverage reached (2) is a thoroughness measure for finishing, and the smoke test (3) is about starting.
distractorNotes.C: The smoke test (3) checks the initial quality of the test object before starting: an entry criterion.
distractorNotes.D: Mixed up: an available environment (1) is a precondition for starting.

stem: On the release date of a mobile card game, 15% of the planned tests have not been run. The product owner reviews the remaining risks and agrees to release. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: Testing can never end until every planned test has been run
The exit criteria were met because the release date is an entry criterion
Running out of time can be a valid exit criterion if the stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the risk of going live without further testing
The testers must block the release, because only testers decide when testing ends
why: The syllabus allows running out of time or budget as an exit criterion when stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the risk.

distractorNotes.A: Overgeneralisation: exhaustive completion of the plan is not the only way to finish.
distractorNotes.B: Confused: a release date is not an entry criterion, and this does not make the other exit criteria met.
distractorNotes.D: Wrong actor: stakeholders accept the risk; testers inform the decision.

stem: In a mobile studio's Scrum team, a story may only be taken into a sprint once it has acceptance criteria, mock-ups and an estimate. What is this set of conditions usually called?
options: The Definition of Ready
The Definition of Done
The test completion criteria
The acceptance criteria
why: In Agile, the entry criteria a user story must meet before development or testing starts are called the Definition of Ready.

distractorNotes.B: Adjacent-concept swap: the Definition of Done is the exit side.
distractorNotes.C: Completion is about finishing; these conditions are about starting work on the story.
distractorNotes.D: Acceptance criteria describe what the story must do; here they are only one of the conditions for starting.

stem: Which of the following is a measure of thoroughness used as an exit criterion?
options: Availability of test data
Defect density
All smoke tests have passed
Static testing has been performed
why: Measures of thoroughness include achieved coverage, number of unresolved defects, defect density and number of failed test cases.

distractorNotes.A: Availability of resources is an entry criterion.
distractorNotes.C: The initial quality level of the test object is an entry criterion.
distractorNotes.D: This IS an exit criterion, but a binary yes/no one, not a measure of thoroughness.

stem: The integration test team for a racing game will only start once the component tests of the physics module have passed with 100% statement coverage. For the integration test team, what is this condition?
options: An exit criterion
A Definition of Done for the integration tests
A test completion report item
An entry criterion
why: For the integration test team it is a precondition for starting their activity, so it is an entry criterion (for component testing the same condition is an exit criterion).

distractorNotes.A: It is an exit criterion for component testing, but the question asks what it is for the integration test team, which is about to start.
distractorNotes.B: The Definition of Done is the exit side of the integration work, not its precondition.
distractorNotes.C: A completion report summarises results at the end; this is a condition for starting.

stem: Using three-point estimation, a tester estimates the effort to test a new photo mode: optimistic 2, most likely 5, pessimistic 14 person-days. What is the estimate E?
options: 2 person-days
5 person-days
6 person-days
7 person-days

distractorNotes.A: This is the standard deviation (14 − 2) / 6 = 2, not the estimate.
distractorNotes.B: This is only the most likely value m.
distractorNotes.D: The plain average (2 + 5 + 14) / 3 = 7; the most likely value must count four times and the sum is divided by 6.

stem: For testing a seasonal event, the experts give: optimistic 3, most likely 6, pessimistic 21 person-days. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimate with its standard deviation?
options: 6 ± 3 person-days
8 ± 3 person-days
8 ± 18 person-days
10 ± 3 person-days

distractorNotes.A: 6 is only the most likely value m.
distractorNotes.C: 18 is b - a; the standard deviation divides it by 6.
distractorNotes.D: 10 is the plain average (3 + 6 + 21) / 3, not the weighted three-point estimate.

stem: In a studio's earlier projects, every 5 person-days of development needed 2 person-days of testing. A new expansion needs 350 person-days of development. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the test effort?
options: 70 person-days
140 person-days
175 person-days
875 person-days
why: Ratio 5 : 2 (development : test). Test = 350 × 2 / 5 = 140.

distractorNotes.A: 350 / 5: the number of 5-day blocks, not multiplied by the 2 test days per block.
distractorNotes.C: 350 / 2: the ratio was applied as if testing were half of development.
distractorNotes.D: 350 × 5 / 2: the ratio was turned the wrong way round.

stem: The first four sprints of a new roguelike needed 18, 22, 20 and 24 person-days of testing. The team forecasts the next sprint by extrapolation, using the average of the sprints so far. What is the estimate?
options: 21 person-days
24 person-days
26 person-days
84 person-days

distractorNotes.B: This is only the latest sprint, not the average.
distractorNotes.C: Assumes the effort keeps rising by 2 per sprint; the stem asks for the average.
distractorNotes.D: This is the total of the four sprints, not the average per sprint.

stem: A test manager asks four senior testers to estimate the effort for a new co-op mode, each on their own. She collects the numbers, asks the two whose estimates are far from the rest to explain, and then everyone estimates again, alone, until the numbers converge. Which technique is this?
options: Three-point estimation
Extrapolation
Estimation based on ratios
Wideband Delphi
why: Experts estimating in isolation, discussing outliers and repeating rounds until consensus is Wideband Delphi.

distractorNotes.A: Three-point estimation uses an optimistic, a most likely and a pessimistic value; it has no repeated rounds.
distractorNotes.B: Extrapolation is metrics-based: it extends measurements from the current project.
distractorNotes.C: Ratio estimation is metrics-based: it uses ratios from earlier projects.

stem: A team uses the test effort measured in the first two iterations of the current project to forecast the third iteration. Which estimation technique is this?
options: Extrapolation
Estimation based on ratios
Wideband Delphi
Planning Poker
why: Extrapolation uses measurements made as early as possible in the current project.

distractorNotes.B: Ratios come from previous projects in the organisation, not from early iterations of this one.
distractorNotes.C: Wideband Delphi is expert-based, with rounds of independent estimates.
distractorNotes.D: Planning Poker is the Agile variant of Wideband Delphi: expert-based, not measurement-based.

stem: Which statement about the four estimation techniques is CORRECT?
options: Estimation based on ratios and Wideband Delphi are metrics-based; extrapolation and three-point estimation are expert-based
All four are expert-based, because people always choose the numbers
Estimation based on ratios and extrapolation are metrics-based; Wideband Delphi and three-point estimation are expert-based
Three-point estimation is metrics-based, because it uses a formula
why: Ratios and extrapolation use data; Wideband Delphi and three-point estimation use expert judgement.

distractorNotes.A: Wideband Delphi is expert-based, and extrapolation is metrics-based.
distractorNotes.B: Category smear: ratios and extrapolation are driven by measured data.
distractorNotes.D: Using a formula does not make it metrics-based: the three values come from experts.

stem: For a new quest editor, three-point estimation gave E = 14 person-days. The optimistic estimate was 6 and the pessimistic estimate was 30. What was the most likely estimate?
options: 12 person-days
14 person-days
18 person-days
48 person-days

distractorNotes.B: 14 is E itself; the most likely value is not the same as the weighted estimate when a and b are not symmetric around it.
distractorNotes.C: 18 is the midpoint of 6 and 30, which ignores the formula.
distractorNotes.D: 48 is 4m; it still has to be divided by 4.

stem: In a studio's last three titles, development and testing effort had a ratio of 7 : 3. The new title needs 420 person-days of development. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the TOTAL effort for development and testing together?
options: 180 person-days
600 person-days
980 person-days
1400 person-days

distractorNotes.A: This is the test effort alone; the question asks for the total.
distractorNotes.C: 420 × 7 / 3: the ratio turned the wrong way round, giving a (wrong) test effort only.
distractorNotes.D: 420 + 980: development plus a test effort from the inverted ratio.

stem: Experts estimate the testing of a new photo-sharing feature at optimistic 5, most likely 8 and pessimistic 23 person-days. Using three-point estimation, which range is given by the estimate plus or minus one standard deviation?
options: 5 to 23 person-days
5 to 11 person-days
7 to 13 person-days
9 to 15 person-days

distractorNotes.A: This is just the optimistic to pessimistic range.
distractorNotes.B: Centred on the most likely value 8 instead of the estimate 10.
distractorNotes.D: Centred on the plain average (5 + 8 + 23) / 3 = 12 instead of the weighted estimate 10.

stem: During Planning Poker for a story about guild chat, two testers show 3 and 13 while everyone else shows 5. Following the Wideband Delphi approach, what should happen next?
options: The average of all the cards is taken as the estimate
The testers with the outlying estimates explain their reasoning, then everyone estimates again
The product owner chooses the final number
The highest card is taken, to be on the safe side
why: Planning Poker is a variant of Wideband Delphi: outliers explain, and the experts re-estimate until they converge.

distractorNotes.A: Averaging skips the discussion and re-estimation that bring hidden assumptions to light.
distractorNotes.C: Wrong actor: the estimate comes from the people doing the work reaching consensus.
distractorNotes.D: Picking a card without discussion is not the technique; it may also hide a misunderstanding.

stem: A test lead orders the test cases for a battle-royale patch so that the tests for areas with the highest likelihood times impact run first. Which prioritisation strategy is this?
options: Coverage-based prioritisation
Risk-based prioritisation
Requirements-based prioritisation
Additional coverage-based prioritisation
why: Ordering by the results of risk analysis (likelihood and impact) is risk-based prioritisation.

distractorNotes.A: Coverage-based ordering uses code or requirements coverage, not risk levels.
distractorNotes.C: Requirements-based ordering uses stakeholder priorities of the requirements.
distractorNotes.D: This is a coverage-based variant: each next test adds the most uncovered coverage.

stem: The product owner of a cooking game ranks the requirements by business importance, and the test cases traced to the top-ranked requirements are run first. Which prioritisation strategy is this?
options: Requirements-based prioritisation
Risk-based prioritisation
Coverage-based prioritisation
Additional coverage-based prioritisation
why: Ordering tests by the stakeholder-defined priorities of the requirements they trace to is requirements-based prioritisation.

distractorNotes.B: Risk-based ordering uses likelihood and impact from risk analysis.
distractorNotes.C: Coverage-based ordering uses how much code or how many requirements a test covers.
distractorNotes.D: Additional coverage-based ordering picks each next test by the coverage it adds.

stem: Five test cases have these priorities (1 = highest): TC1 priority 2; TC2 priority 4; TC3 priority 1, depends on TC5; TC4 priority 3; TC5 priority 5. The rule is: run the highest-priority test as early as possible; a test it depends on runs right before it. In which order are the tests run?
options: TC3, TC1, TC4, TC2, TC5
TC1, TC4, TC2, TC5, TC3
TC5, TC1, TC3, TC4, TC2
TC5, TC3, TC1, TC4, TC2
why: TC3 is the top priority but needs TC5, so TC5 then TC3. Then by priority: TC1 (2), TC4 (3), TC2 (4).

distractorNotes.A: Pure priority order: TC3 cannot run before TC5, which it depends on.
distractorNotes.B: Each step takes the highest-priority test that is ready, so the top-priority TC3 runs last; the stated rule runs it as early as possible.
distractorNotes.C: TC3 is delayed after TC1 although its dependency has already run.

stem: Test cases for a heist game have these priorities (1 = highest): A priority 1, depends on B; B priority 3, depends on C; C priority 5; D priority 2; E priority 4. The rule is: run the highest-priority test as early as possible; tests it depends on run right before it. In which order are the tests run?
options: A, D, B, E, C
B, C, A, D, E
C, B, A, D, E
D, E, C, B, A
why: A needs B, and B needs C, so the chain C, B, A runs first. Then D (2) and E (4).

distractorNotes.A: Pure priority order ignores the dependencies: A cannot run before B and C.
distractorNotes.B: B depends on C, so C must run before B.
distractorNotes.D: Taking the highest-priority test that is ready at each step delays the top-priority A to the end; the stated rule runs it as early as possible.

stem: Six requirements, R1 to R6, are covered by four tests: T1 covers R1, R2, R3, R4; T2 covers R1, R2, R5; T3 covers R5, R6; T4 covers R3, R4, R6. Using additional coverage-based prioritisation, which test runs SECOND?
options: T2
T3
T4
T1
why: T1 runs first (4 requirements). Then the extra coverage: T2 adds R5 (1), T3 adds R5 and R6 (2), T4 adds R6 (1). T3 adds the most.

distractorNotes.A: T2 has the second-highest total coverage (3), but after T1 it adds only R5.
distractorNotes.C: T4 also covers 3 requirements in total, but after T1 it adds only R6.
distractorNotes.D: T1 runs first, as it has the highest coverage.

stem: A level's code has ten statements, S1 to S10. Test TA covers S1 to S5; TB covers S6 and S7; TC covers S5, S6 and S8; TD covers S8, S9 and S10. Using additional coverage-based prioritisation, in which order are the tests run?
options: TA, TD, TB, TC
TA, TC, TD, TB
TA, TD, TC, TB
TD, TA, TB, TC
why: TA first (5). Then TB adds 2, TC adds 2 (S6, S8), TD adds 3 (S8, S9, S10): TD. Then TB adds 2 (S6, S7) and TC adds 1 (S6): TB. TC last.

distractorNotes.B: Ordered by total coverage (5, 3, 3, 2), not by the coverage each test adds.
distractorNotes.C: The second step is right, but at the third step TB adds two new statements (S6, S7) and TC only one (S6).
distractorNotes.D: TA has the highest coverage, so it runs first.

stem: Four product risks for a racing game are rated on 1–5 scales, and risk level = likelihood × impact: A likelihood 3, impact 4; B likelihood 5, impact 3; C likelihood 2, impact 5; D likelihood 4, impact 4. Using risk-based prioritisation, in which order are their tests run?
options: B, D, A, C
C, D, A, B
C, A, B, D
D, B, A, C
why: Levels: A 12, B 15, C 10, D 16. Highest first: D, B, A, C.

distractorNotes.A: Ordered by likelihood alone (5, 4, 3, 2).
distractorNotes.B: Ordered by impact alone (5, 4, 4, 3).
distractorNotes.C: Lowest risk level first: the reverse of risk-based ordering.

stem: Five test cases each take one hour: T1 priority 1, T2 priority 2, T3 priority 3, T4 priority 4, T5 priority 5 (1 = highest). No test depends on another. T3 needs the studio's only VR headset, which is free in hour 1 only. What is the best order?
why: Resource availability can change the order: T3 must use the headset's only free hour, so it runs first; the rest follow by priority.

distractorNotes.A: Strict priority order puts T3 in hour 3, when the headset is not available.
distractorNotes.B: In hour 2 the headset is no longer free.
distractorNotes.D: T3 first is right, but the rest should follow priority order, not the reverse.

stem: Which statement about test case prioritisation is CORRECT?
options: Test cases must always run strictly in order of priority
In requirements-based prioritisation, the testers set the priorities of the requirements
If a higher-priority test depends on a lower-priority test, the lower-priority test must be run first
Coverage-based prioritisation runs the test with the lowest coverage first, so gaps are found early
why: Dependencies come before priority: the test that others depend on must run before them.

distractorNotes.A: Overgeneralisation: dependencies and resource availability can change the order.
distractorNotes.B: Wrong actor: stakeholders define the requirement priorities.
distractorNotes.D: The wrong way round: the test with the highest coverage runs first.

stem: Six test cases (1 = highest priority): T1 priority 1, depends on T4 and T6; T2 priority 2; T3 priority 3, depends on T5; T4 priority 6; T5 priority 4; T6 priority 5. The rule is: run the highest-priority test as early as possible; tests it depends on run right before it. Which test runs FIFTH?
options: T3
T5
T6
T2
why: T4 and T6 run first (in either order), then T1, then T2 (2). Next is T3 (3), which needs T5, so T5 runs fifth and T3 sixth.

distractorNotes.A: T3 depends on T5, so T5 must run before it: T3 is sixth.
distractorNotes.C: Fifth in pure priority order (T1, T2, T3, T5, T6, T4), which ignores the dependencies.
distractorNotes.D: T2 runs fourth, straight after T1.

stem: Four automated tests for a platformer achieve this statement coverage on their own: T1 45%, T2 70%, T3 30%, T4 60%. Using coverage-based prioritisation, which test runs first?
options: T2
T3
T4
T1
why: Coverage-based prioritisation runs the test with the highest coverage first: T2 with 70%.

distractorNotes.B: The lowest coverage: the wrong way round.
distractorNotes.C: The second-highest coverage.
distractorNotes.D: Neither highest nor lowest; the numbering is not the order.

stem: Which statement about the test pyramid is CORRECT?
options: The higher layers hold the most tests, because they are closest to the user
Tests in the lower layers are the most expensive per test
The pyramid shows the order in which the test levels are executed
Tests in the lower layers are smaller, more isolated and faster than tests in the higher layers
why: The higher the layer, the lower the granularity, isolation and execution speed, and the higher the cost.

distractorNotes.A: The wrong way round: the top holds the fewest tests.
distractorNotes.B: Cost rises towards the top of the pyramid.
distractorNotes.C: It shows granularity and how many tests to have per layer, not a sequence.

stem: What does the test pyramid support a team in?
options: Defect classification and triage
Test automation and test effort allocation
Running product risk identification workshops
Estimating test effort from earlier projects' ratios
why: The pyramid supports the team in test automation and in allocating test effort, by showing the goals of different levels of automated tests.

distractorNotes.A: That is defect management (5.5).
distractorNotes.C: That is risk analysis (5.2).
distractorNotes.D: That is an estimation technique (5.1.4).

stem: A team's automated suite for a strategy game has 40 end-to-end UI tests, 15 service tests and 5 unit tests. Which statement fits the test pyramid?
options: This matches the pyramid, because end-to-end tests are the closest to the players
The pyramid recommends the same number of tests in every layer
The shape is inverted: the model suggests many small, fast, isolated tests at the bottom and only a few end-to-end tests at the top
The pyramid only applies to manual tests, so it says nothing about this suite
why: Lower layers need many tests for reasonable coverage; the slow, expensive end-to-end tests at the top should be few.

distractorNotes.A: Closeness to the user does not mean more tests; the top layer should be the smallest.
distractorNotes.B: It recommends many at the bottom and few at the top.
distractorNotes.D: The pyramid is about automated tests of different granularity.

stem: Moving UP the test pyramid, how do the tests change?
options: Granularity, isolation and execution speed go down, and cost goes up
Granularity, isolation and execution speed go down, and cost goes down
Isolation and execution speed go up, and cost goes up
Granularity and cost go down, and execution speed goes up
why: Higher layers have lower test granularity, lower isolation, slower execution and higher cost.

distractorNotes.B: Cost goes up towards the top.
distractorNotes.C: Isolation and speed go down towards the top.
distractorNotes.D: Cost rises and speed falls towards the top.

stem: Which layers does the original test pyramid model have?
options: Component testing, system testing and acceptance testing
Q1, Q2 and Q3
Static, dynamic and exploratory tests
Unit tests, service tests and UI tests
why: The original model has unit, service and UI layers; other versions use names such as component, integration and end-to-end.

distractorNotes.A: These are test levels, not the original pyramid layers.
distractorNotes.B: These are testing quadrants, a different model (and there are four of them).
distractorNotes.C: These are not layers of the pyramid.

stem: Which test belongs at the TOP of the test pyramid?
options: A test of the XP-curve function with fifty input values
A test that one C# class saves and loads its fields correctly
An automated test that buys a skin in the live store with a test account and checks it appears in the player's locker on another device
A test of the inventory and crafting components talking through a mock
why: The top layer holds complex, high-level end-to-end tests that check a large piece of functionality.

distractorNotes.A: A small, isolated, fast check of one function: the bottom layer.
distractorNotes.B: A unit test: the bottom layer.
distractorNotes.D: A component integration (service-level) test: the middle layer.

stem: In which testing quadrant are component tests and component integration tests?
options: Q1: technology facing, supporting the team
Q2: business facing, supporting the team
Q3: business facing, critiquing the product
Q4: technology facing, critiquing the product
why: Q1 holds component and component integration tests; they should be automated and part of CI.

distractorNotes.B: Q2 holds functional tests, examples, story tests, UX prototypes, API tests and simulations.
distractorNotes.C: Q3 holds exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing.
distractorNotes.D: Q4 holds smoke tests and non-functional tests except usability.

stem: Players try a new heads-up display in a lab while the team watches how easily they find their ammo count. In which testing quadrant is this test?
options: Q4: technology facing, critiquing the product
Q3: business facing, critiquing the product
Q2: business facing, supporting the team
Q1: technology facing, supporting the team
why: Usability testing is in Q3, with exploratory testing and user acceptance testing.

distractorNotes.A: Trap: usability is non-functional, but Q4 is non-functional testing EXCEPT usability.
distractorNotes.C: Q2 tests check acceptance criteria while building; this judges the product with users.
distractorNotes.D: Q1 is component-level testing.

stem: An automated benchmark simulates a 200-unit battle and measures whether the game stays at 60 frames per second on the minimum-spec PC. In which testing quadrant is this test?
options: Q2: business facing, supporting the team
Q3: business facing, critiquing the product
Q1: technology facing, supporting the team
Q4: technology facing, critiquing the product
why: Performance tests are non-functional (not usability), so they are in Q4.

distractorNotes.A: Trap: Q2 lists "simulations", but this simulation only drives a performance measurement: a non-functional test of the technology.
distractorNotes.B: Q3 is user-oriented testing: exploratory, usability, user acceptance.
distractorNotes.C: Q1 is component and component integration testing.

stem: A tester writes automated API tests for the in-game store's purchase endpoint, checking the acceptance criteria of the story "a player can buy a bundle with gems". In which testing quadrant are these tests?
options: Q1: technology facing, supporting the team
Q4: technology facing, critiquing the product
Q2: business facing, supporting the team
Q3: business facing, critiquing the product
why: The syllabus places API testing in Q2, with functional tests, examples and user story tests that check acceptance criteria.

distractorNotes.A: Trap: API tests feel technical, but Q1 is component and component integration testing.
distractorNotes.B: Q4 is smoke and non-functional testing.
distractorNotes.D: Q3 is exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing.

stem: What is the main purpose of the testing quadrants?
options: To help make sure all appropriate test types and test levels are included, and to explain the kinds of tests to stakeholders
To decide how many automated tests of each granularity to write
To rank product risks by likelihood and impact
To define the order in which test cases are run
why: The quadrants group test levels with test types, activities, techniques and work products, so test management can check nothing is missing and describe the tests to stakeholders.

distractorNotes.B: That is the test pyramid.
distractorNotes.C: That is risk assessment.
distractorNotes.D: That is test case prioritisation.

stem: Which statement about the testing quadrants is CORRECT?
options: Q3 tests are usually fully automated
Q1 tests should be automated and included in the continuous integration process
Q4 includes usability testing
Q2 tests critique the product
why: Component and component integration tests (Q1) should be automated and run in CI.

distractorNotes.A: Q3 tests are user-oriented and often manual.
distractorNotes.C: Q4 is non-functional testing except usability; usability is Q3.
distractorNotes.D: Q2 tests support the team.

stem: After every nightly build, an automated check confirms the game launches, loads the hub world and connects to the servers. In which testing quadrant is this test?
options: Q1: technology facing, supporting the team
Q2: business facing, supporting the team
Q3: business facing, critiquing the product
Q4: technology facing, critiquing the product
why: Smoke tests are listed in Q4, with non-functional tests (except usability).

distractorNotes.A: It is automated and technical, but Q1 holds component and component integration tests.
distractorNotes.B: Q2 holds functional and story tests that check acceptance criteria.
distractorNotes.C: Q3 is user-oriented, often manual testing.

stem: Match each test to its quadrant: 1. User acceptance testing by a guild of beta players. 2. Unit tests on the loot drop function. 3. Given/When/Then tests for a user story. 4. A security vulnerability scan of the servers.
why: User acceptance testing is Q3; unit tests are Q1; user story tests are Q2; security is a non-functional test, so Q4.

distractorNotes.A: User acceptance testing critiques the product (Q3), and story tests support the team (Q2).
distractorNotes.B: Unit tests support the team (Q1); a security scan critiques the product (Q4).
distractorNotes.D: User acceptance testing is business facing (Q3), and security is non-functional (Q4).

stem: Which two factors determine the level of a risk?
options: Risk impact and the cost of testing
Risk likelihood and risk impact
Risk likelihood and the number of test cases
Severity and priority
why: Risk level is expressed by the likelihood of the risk and its impact if it happens.

distractorNotes.A: The cost of testing is not a risk attribute.
distractorNotes.C: The number of tests is a response, not an attribute of the risk.
distractorNotes.D: Adjacent-concept swap: these are attributes of a defect, not of a risk.

stem: Four risks for a fighting game are rated on 1–5 scales, and risk level = likelihood × impact. Which has the HIGHEST risk level?
options: Likelihood 4, impact 3
Likelihood 2, impact 5
Likelihood 5, impact 2
Likelihood 3, impact 3

distractorNotes.B: Level 10: the highest impact alone does not give the highest level.
distractorNotes.C: Level 10: the highest likelihood alone does not give the highest level.
distractorNotes.D: Level 9.

stem: Which statement about risk likelihood is CORRECT?
options: It is the harm caused if the risk occurs
It equals 1 for a risk that is already happening
It can only be set after the risk has occurred
It is a probability greater than zero and less than one
why: Risk likelihood is the probability of the risk occurring, more than 0 and less than 1.

distractorNotes.A: That is risk impact.
distractorNotes.B: Something that is certain or already happening is an issue, not a risk.
distractorNotes.C: Likelihood is assessed before, during risk analysis.

stem: Risk P: a very unlikely event that would corrupt every save file. Risk Q: a very likely event that would misalign one tooltip. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: P is always the higher risk, because impact decides the risk level
Q is always the higher risk, because likelihood decides the risk level
Their risk levels depend on both likelihood and impact, so neither is automatically the higher risk
Neither is a risk, because one is unlikely and the other is harmless
why: Risk level combines likelihood and impact; without the full assessment neither risk wins by one factor alone.

distractorNotes.A: Impact alone does not set the risk level.
distractorNotes.B: Likelihood alone does not set the risk level.
distractorNotes.D: Both have a likelihood above zero and some impact, so both are risks.

stem: Risk X has a likelihood of 10% and an impact of 80,000 euros. Risk Y has a likelihood of 40% and an impact of 25,000 euros. Using risk level = likelihood × impact, which statement is CORRECT?
options: X has the higher risk level, because its impact is higher
Neither can be compared, because risk levels need a qualitative risk matrix
Neither is a risk, because both likelihoods are below 50%
Y has the higher risk level: 10,000 against 8,000

distractorNotes.A: Impact alone: it ignores that Y is four times as likely.
distractorNotes.B: Risk levels can be quantitative (likelihood × impact) or qualitative.
distractorNotes.C: Any likelihood above zero (and below one) makes it a risk.

stem: What does a higher risk level mean for the risk?
options: It needs less testing, because it is already well understood
It is more important to treat it
It is a project risk rather than a product risk
It has already occurred
why: The higher the risk level, the more important its treatment.

distractorNotes.A: The opposite: higher risk usually gets more attention.
distractorNotes.C: Risk level says nothing about whether it is a project or product risk.
distractorNotes.D: A risk that has occurred is an issue; risk level is about potential events.

stem: Which of the following is a project risk?
options: The external motion-capture studio may deliver the animations three weeks late
The in-game clock may show the wrong time after a daylight-saving change
Matchmaking may take more than five seconds at peak times
The chat filter may let offensive words through
why: A supplier failing to deliver on time threatens the schedule: a project risk (supplier issue).

distractorNotes.B: Wrong behaviour of the product: a product risk.
distractorNotes.C: Inadequate response time: a product risk.
distractorNotes.D: Wrong functionality of the product: a product risk.

stem: Which of the following is a product risk?
options: The test lead may be moved to another project
The test budget may be cut by 20%
The vendor of the test management tool may stop supporting it
Players may clip through walls at very high frame rates
why: A runtime defect in the game's behaviour is a product risk.

distractorNotes.A: A people issue: a project risk.
distractorNotes.B: An organisational issue (cost-cutting): a project risk.
distractorNotes.C: A supplier / tool support issue: a project risk.

stem: Classify these risks: 1. Too few testers with console experience. 2. Inefficient pathfinding causing frame drops. 3. New features keep being added to the scope. 4. A security hole in the login service.
options: 1 and 2 are project risks; 3 and 4 are product risks
1 and 3 are project risks; 2 and 4 are product risks
Only 1 is a project risk; 2, 3 and 4 are product risks
2 and 4 are project risks; 1 and 3 are product risks
why: Staff shortage (people) and scope creep (technical) threaten the project; inefficient algorithms and security vulnerabilities are product quality risks.

distractorNotes.A: Inefficient pathfinding (2) is about the product's quality, and scope creep (3) is a project risk.
distractorNotes.C: Scope creep (3) is listed as a project risk (technical issue).
distractorNotes.D: Swapped: performance and security are product quality characteristics.

stem: If a project risk occurs, what does it typically affect?
options: Player satisfaction and the studio's reputation
Criminal penalties for a data breach
The project's schedule, budget or scope
High maintenance costs and an overloaded help desk
why: Project risks, when they occur, affect schedule, budget or scope, and so the project's ability to reach its objectives.

distractorNotes.A: These are typical consequences of product risks.
distractorNotes.B: A consequence of a product risk (security).
distractorNotes.D: Consequences of product risks.

stem: The team's test automation tool does not support the new console's SDK yet. What kind of risk is this?
options: A project risk: a technical issue (poor tool support)
A product risk, because it is a technical problem
A product risk, because it may let defects reach players
Not a risk, because tool problems are only issues
why: Poor tool support is a technical project risk: it threatens the schedule and the testing effort, not the game's quality characteristics directly.

distractorNotes.B: Category smear: 'technical' does not make it a product risk; tool support is a project matter.
distractorNotes.C: The tool is not part of the product; the risk is to the project's ability to test.
distractorNotes.D: It is a potential event with an adverse effect, so it is a risk.

stem: Which of the following is a typical consequence of a PRODUCT risk occurring?
options: The test team misses its milestone
The budget overruns by 15%
An overloaded help desk after launch
The scope of the release is reduced
why: Product risks can lead to user dissatisfaction, lost revenue or reputation, damage to third parties, high maintenance costs and an overloaded help desk, penalties or even harm.

distractorNotes.A: A schedule impact: a consequence of a project risk.
distractorNotes.B: A budget impact: a consequence of a project risk.
distractorNotes.D: A scope impact: a consequence of a project risk.

stem: Two senior developers on a survival game do not speak to each other and keep breaking each other's interface agreements. How is this risk best classified?
options: A product risk: an architecture issue
A project risk: a people issue
A project risk: a supplier issue
A product risk: a functional suitability issue
why: Conflicts and communication problems between people are people issues, a kind of project risk.

distractorNotes.A: The source of the risk is how people work together, not the product's architecture.
distractorNotes.C: No third party is involved.
distractorNotes.D: The risk described is about people and communication, not the product's functions.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a product risk?
options: Save files may grow too large for the cloud storage quota
Colour-blind players may not tell the two teams apart
Damage may be rounded down wrongly for fractional values
The test estimates for the expansion may be too optimistic
why: Inaccurate estimates are an organisational issue: a project risk. The other three are about the product's quality.

distractorNotes.A: This IS a product risk (the product's behaviour with data).
distractorNotes.B: This IS a product risk (usability / user experience).
distractorNotes.C: This IS a product risk (incorrect calculation).

stem: Which two activities make up product risk analysis?
options: Risk identification and risk assessment
Risk mitigation and risk monitoring
Risk transfer and risk acceptance
Test planning and test estimation
why: Product risk analysis consists of risk identification and risk assessment.

distractorNotes.B: Adjacent-concept swap: these make up risk control.
distractorNotes.C: These are response options, part of risk control.
distractorNotes.D: These are planning activities, not the parts of risk analysis.

stem: In a workshop, the team takes the list of risks for a new trading feature, decides how likely and how harmful each one is, and sorts them. Which activity is this?
options: Risk identification
Risk mitigation
Risk assessment
Risk monitoring
why: Determining likelihood, impact and level, and prioritising the risks, is risk assessment.

distractorNotes.A: Identification builds the list; here the list already exists and is being rated.
distractorNotes.B: Mitigation carries out actions to reduce the risks; nothing is being done to them yet.
distractorNotes.D: Monitoring checks that mitigation works and looks for new risks.

stem: Which of the following is a way the results of product risk analysis influence testing?
options: They decide which developer fixes each defect
They set the severity of each defect found
They choose the marketing date of the release
They help determine which test techniques to use and what coverage to reach
why: Risk analysis results are used to set scope, test levels and types, techniques and coverage, effort and priorities, and other risk-reducing activities.

distractorNotes.A: Assigning fixes is defect management, not test scoping.
distractorNotes.B: Severity is set per defect in the defect report.
distractorNotes.C: Not an influence of product risk analysis on testing.

stem: What is the goal of product risk analysis?
options: To remove all product risks before release
To focus the test effort so that the residual level of product risk is minimised
To prove that the product has no defects
To replace test planning in risk-based testing
why: Product risk analysis gives awareness of product risk so that testing reduces the residual risk as much as possible.

distractorNotes.A: Overgeneralisation: testing reduces risk; it cannot remove all of it.
distractorNotes.C: Testing cannot prove the absence of defects.
distractorNotes.D: Risk analysis feeds planning; it does not replace it.

stem: Why is it useful to categorise identified product risks during risk assessment?
options: Risks in the same category can often be mitigated in a similar way
Categorised risks no longer need a likelihood or impact
Categorisation makes risk identification unnecessary
Only categorised risks can be tested
why: Categorisation helps assign mitigation actions, because risks in one category usually share an approach.

distractorNotes.B: Assessment still rates likelihood and impact.
distractorNotes.C: You can only categorise risks that were identified first.
distractorNotes.D: Invented restriction.

stem: Product risk analysis for a puzzle game rates "progress lost when switching between phone and PC" as its highest risk. Which consequence for testing is the most appropriate?
options: Leave it to the developers, because high-risk areas are usually tested by them anyway
Test it last, after the lower-risk areas have shown the build is stable
Give it high severity in a defect report
Add cross-platform compatibility tests, run them early, and plan more effort for them
why: A high product risk should shape test types, priority (find critical defects early) and the effort estimated.

distractorNotes.A: Ignores the analysis: high risk calls for more focused testing, not less.
distractorNotes.B: Risk-based testing tests the highest risks first, to find critical defects early.
distractorNotes.C: Severity belongs to defects found, not to a risk before testing.

stem: Which of the following can be used for product risk identification?
options: Three-point estimation
Burn-down charts
Brainstorming and interviews with stakeholders
Statement coverage
why: Risk identification techniques include brainstorming, workshops, interviews and cause-effect diagrams.

distractorNotes.A: An estimation technique (5.1.4).
distractorNotes.B: A way to communicate test status (5.3.3).
distractorNotes.D: A white-box coverage measure (4.3).

stem: Which two activities make up product risk control?
options: Risk identification and risk assessment
Risk mitigation and risk monitoring
Risk acceptance and risk transfer
Test estimation and test prioritisation
why: Product risk control consists of risk mitigation and risk monitoring.

distractorNotes.A: Adjacent-concept swap: these make up risk analysis.
distractorNotes.C: These are response options, not the two parts of risk control.
distractorNotes.D: These are planning activities (5.1).

stem: A publisher's contract states that the porting partner pays for any defects found on their platform after launch. Which response to the product risk is this?
options: Risk transfer
Risk mitigation by testing
Risk acceptance
A contingency plan
why: Moving the consequences of a risk to another party (here by contract) is risk transfer.

distractorNotes.B: No testing is being done to reduce the risk level.
distractorNotes.C: The risk is not simply lived with; its cost is moved to someone else.
distractorNotes.D: A contingency plan prepares actions if the risk happens; this moves who bears it.

stem: A typo may remain in one optional lore book in the Portuguese version. The team rates it as very low risk and decides to ship without doing anything about it. Which response is this?
options: Risk transfer
Risk mitigation by testing
A contingency plan
Risk acceptance
why: Deciding to live with an assessed risk is risk acceptance.

distractorNotes.A: Nobody else takes on the risk.
distractorNotes.B: No action reduces the risk.
distractorNotes.C: No plan is prepared for if it happens.

stem: Before an esports final, the team writes a step-by-step plan for switching the match to an offline LAN setup, with a backup referee tool, in case the online servers fail. Which response is this?
options: Risk acceptance
Risk transfer
A contingency plan
Risk monitoring
why: Preparing what to do if the risk occurs is a contingency plan.

distractorNotes.A: The team does more than live with the risk: it prepares a response.
distractorNotes.B: No other party takes on the risk.
distractorNotes.D: Monitoring checks mitigation and watches for new risks; this prepares for the event happening.

stem: Which of the following is a way to mitigate a product risk BY TESTING?
options: Signing a contract that makes the hosting provider pay for any downtime
Having the new matchmaking rules tested by a team that did not build them
Deciding to live with a minor risk
Adding the risk to the risk register
why: Applying an appropriate level of independence of testing is a listed way to mitigate product risks by testing.

distractorNotes.A: Risk transfer, not testing.
distractorNotes.C: Risk acceptance, not testing.
distractorNotes.D: That records the risk (identification); it does not reduce it.

stem: After the mitigation tests on a game's trading system are done, the QA lead checks the crash reports and player complaints to see whether the tests worked and whether any new risks appear. Which activity is this?
options: Risk monitoring
Risk mitigation
Risk assessment
Risk identification
why: Checking that mitigation actions are effective, and identifying emerging risks, is risk monitoring.

distractorNotes.B: Mitigation carried out the actions; checking their effect is monitoring.
distractorNotes.C: Assessment rates likelihood and impact in risk analysis.
distractorNotes.D: Trap: spotting emerging risks after mitigation is part of risk monitoring in risk control.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an action to mitigate product risks by testing?
options: Performing static analysis on the networking code
Using 3-value boundary value analysis on the damage ranges
Adding regression tests for the patched quest system
Moving the release date back by two weeks
why: Changing the release date is a project decision, not a test action. The other three are listed testing actions: static analysis, suitable techniques and coverage, and regression testing.

distractorNotes.A: This IS a mitigation action by testing (reviews and static analysis).
distractorNotes.B: This IS a mitigation action by testing (suitable techniques and coverage).
distractorNotes.C: This IS a mitigation action by testing (dynamic testing incl. regression).

stem: Which of the following is a defect metric?
options: Defect detection percentage
Test environment preparation progress
Mean time to failure
Cost of testing
why: Defect metrics include the number and priorities of defects found and fixed, defect density and defect detection percentage.

distractorNotes.B: A test progress metric.
distractorNotes.C: A product quality metric.
distractorNotes.D: A cost metric.

stem: Which of the following is a product quality metric?
options: The number of test cases run
Defect density
The response time of the matchmaking service
Requirements coverage
why: Product quality metrics include availability, response time and mean time to failure.

distractorNotes.A: A test progress metric.
distractorNotes.B: A defect metric.
distractorNotes.D: A coverage metric.

stem: Which of the following is a test progress metric?
options: The residual risk level
The number of test cases passed and failed
The availability of the game servers
The organisational cost of quality
why: Test progress metrics include implementation progress, environment preparation, test cases run/not run and passed/failed, and execution time.

distractorNotes.A: A risk metric.
distractorNotes.C: A product quality metric.
distractorNotes.D: A cost metric.

stem: Match each metric to its group: 1. Code coverage. 2. Residual risk level. 3. Resource usage. 4. Mean time to failure.
options: 1 coverage, 2 risk, 3 cost, 4 defect
1 test progress, 2 risk, 3 project progress, 4 defect
1 coverage, 2 product quality, 3 project progress, 4 risk
1 coverage, 2 risk, 3 project progress, 4 product quality
why: Code coverage is a coverage metric; residual risk is a risk metric; resource usage is a project progress metric; mean time to failure is a product quality metric.

distractorNotes.A: Resource usage is project progress, and MTTF describes product quality, not defects.
distractorNotes.B: Code coverage is a coverage metric, and MTTF is product quality.
distractorNotes.C: Residual risk is a risk metric; MTTF is product quality.

stem: Which of the following is an example of test CONTROL?
options: Counting how many test cases passed this week
Archiving the testware at the end of the project
Adjusting the test schedule because the test environment was delivered late
Recording a failure in a defect report
why: Test control uses monitoring information to take corrective actions (control directives), such as adjusting the schedule after a late environment delivery.

distractorNotes.A: Gathering information is test monitoring.
distractorNotes.B: This happens in test completion.
distractorNotes.D: Defect reporting is part of test execution and defect management.

stem: Which of the following is a cost metric?
options: Test effort
The organisational cost of quality
Test execution time
Number of defects fixed
why: Cost metrics include the cost of testing and the organisational cost of quality.

distractorNotes.A: Trap: effort sounds like cost, but test effort is a project progress metric.
distractorNotes.C: A test progress metric.
distractorNotes.D: A defect metric.

stem: What is the main purpose of a test progress report?
options: To support the ongoing control of testing, with enough information to change the schedule, resources or test plan when needed
To consolidate lessons learned at the end of the project
To replace the test plan once testing has started
To report each individual failure to the developers
why: Progress reports support control: they must make it possible to adjust the schedule, resources or plan when testing deviates.

distractorNotes.B: That is the test completion report.
distractorNotes.C: Progress reports compare against the plan; they do not replace it.
distractorNotes.D: Individual failures are reported in defect reports.

stem: Which item typically appears in a test completion report but NOT in a test progress report?
options: The testing planned for the next period
Impediments to testing and their workarounds
Test metrics
Lessons learned
why: Lessons learned are a completion report item; they look back on a finished stage.

distractorNotes.A: A progress report item only.
distractorNotes.B: Appears in both reports.
distractorNotes.C: Appears in both reports.

stem: Which item typically appears in a test progress report?
options: Lessons learned from the finished test level
The testing planned for the next reporting period
An evaluation of product quality against the exit criteria of the finished level
A list of defects that will stay unfixed at release
why: Progress reports include the test period, progress and deviations, impediments and workarounds, metrics, new and changed risks, and the testing planned for the next period.

distractorNotes.A: A completion report item.
distractorNotes.C: A completion report item.
distractorNotes.D: Defects not fixed at the end are a completion report item.

stem: QA reports to the development team every day in chat, and to the publisher once, at the end, using a set template. Which statement explains this?
options: All stakeholders should receive the same report at the same time
Informal reporting is not allowed by the syllabus
The audience affects the formality and frequency of test reporting
Test completion reports are produced daily
why: Different audiences need different information; reporting within a team is frequent and informal, reporting on a finished project follows a template and happens once.

distractorNotes.A: Reports should be tailored to the audience.
distractorNotes.B: Informal, frequent reporting within a team is normal.
distractorNotes.D: A completion report is produced at the end of a stage.

stem: When is a test completion report prepared?
options: When a project, test level or test type is complete and, ideally, its exit criteria are met
Every day during test execution
Before test planning starts
Whenever a defect report is closed
why: The completion report is prepared during test completion, ideally once the exit criteria are met.

distractorNotes.B: Daily reporting is a progress report.
distractorNotes.C: There is nothing to report on yet.
distractorNotes.D: Closing defects is part of defect management, not a reporting milestone.

stem: A report says: "Week 41. 62% of planned tests run, three days behind because the build was late. Workaround: testing menus on the previous build. New risk: voice chat crashes on two devices. Next week: multiplayer tests." What kind of report is this?
options: A test completion report
A test progress report
A defect report
A test plan
why: A reporting period, progress with deviations, impediments and workarounds, new risks and the testing planned for next week are the content of a progress report.

distractorNotes.A: Trap: it has metrics and risks, but it looks forward (next week) and is for one period of ongoing testing.
distractorNotes.C: A defect report describes one anomaly; this summarises testing.
distractorNotes.D: A plan sets out the approach before testing; this reports on testing under way.

stem: Which statement about test completion reports is CORRECT?
options: They are only written if all exit criteria were met; otherwise no report is made
They list the testing planned for the next reporting period
They are for the test team only, never for other stakeholders
They use the test progress reports and other data, and can provide information for later testing
why: Completion reports draw on progress reports and other data and summarise a stage of testing, which can inform later testing.

distractorNotes.A: Overgeneralisation: the exit criteria should ideally be met, and unmet criteria and unmitigated risks are reported.
distractorNotes.B: That is a progress report item.
distractorNotes.C: Reports are for stakeholders; the audience shapes their form.

stem: Which of the following is a dashboard used to communicate test status?
options: A test charter
A defect report
A burn-down chart
A risk register
why: Dashboards include CI/CD dashboards, task boards and burn-down charts.

distractorNotes.A: A charter guides an exploratory session (4.4).
distractorNotes.B: A defect report describes one anomaly.
distractorNotes.D: A risk register lists risks in the test plan.

stem: A studio outsources its localisation testing to a vendor abroad; the two teams never share an office and meet only in a monthly call. Which way of communicating test status is most appropriate?
options: More formal written communication, such as reports and online documentation
Only short verbal stand-ups, because they are the fastest
No status communication, because the defect tool shows everything
Status only at the end of the project, to avoid interruptions
why: More formal communication may suit distributed teams, where face-to-face talk is not always possible because of distance or time zones.

distractorNotes.B: With no shared office and one call a month, verbal communication alone cannot carry the status.
distractorNotes.C: Status still needs communicating, tailored to the stakeholders.
distractorNotes.D: Ongoing status is needed for control.

stem: Which statement about communicating test status is CORRECT?
options: A formal test report is always the best way
In Agile teams only verbal communication is allowed
Regulatory standards forbid the use of dashboards
The best way depends on things such as test management concerns, the test strategy, regulatory standards or the self-organising team
why: There is no single best option; context decides, and several options can be combined.

distractorNotes.A: Overgeneralisation: it depends on the context and audience.
distractorNotes.B: Agile teams also use dashboards, chat and documentation.
distractorNotes.C: Invented rule.

stem: The studio head wants to know whether the game is ready to release; the developers want to know which automated tests failed last night. What does this show?
options: Both groups should get the same full report
Communication of test status should be tailored to each group of stakeholders
Only the developers need test status
The studio head should read the CI logs
why: Different stakeholders are interested in different information, so communication is tailored.

distractorNotes.A: Different interests call for different content.
distractorNotes.C: Managers need status to make decisions too.
distractorNotes.D: Raw CI logs do not answer a release-readiness question.

stem: Which of the following is an electronic communication channel for test status?
options: Email and chat
A task board
A test completion report
A face-to-face meeting
why: Electronic communication channels include email and chat.

distractorNotes.B: A dashboard.
distractorNotes.C: A formal test report.
distractorNotes.D: Verbal communication.

stem: A rehabilitation game for hospitals must be certified under a medical-device standard. Which way of communicating test status is most appropriate?
options: Verbal updates only, because they are the fastest
Only a CI dashboard, because automated results are objective
Formal test reports, because regulatory standards can decide the means of communication
No status communication until certification
why: Regulatory standards are one of the factors that decide how test status is communicated; certification usually needs formal, documented reports.

distractorNotes.A: Speed does not meet a regulator's need for documented evidence.
distractorNotes.B: A dashboard alone rarely meets regulatory documentation needs.
distractorNotes.D: Ongoing status is still needed, and certification needs records.

stem: In testing, which of the following can be configuration items?
options: Only the source code and the builds
Test cases, test scripts and test logs
Only the approved requirements
Only the defect reports
why: CM in testing covers work products such as test plans, strategies, conditions, cases, scripts, results, logs and reports.

distractorNotes.A: CM also covers testware and test environments.
distractorNotes.C: Too narrow: testware is also managed.
distractorNotes.D: Too narrow: the syllabus lists testware such as cases, scripts and logs.

stem: The test environment for a shooter (build, console firmware, driver versions) was approved for system testing. A tester now wants to update the driver. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: Anyone may update it, because CM only tracks source code
The change is made and the old baseline is deleted
The environment is a baseline, so the change must go through the formal change control process
A baseline can never be changed under any circumstances
why: An approved configuration item becomes a baseline and can only be changed through formal change control.

distractorNotes.A: CM covers test environments too.
distractorNotes.B: CM keeps records so earlier baselines can be restored.
distractorNotes.D: Overgeneralisation: it can change, through formal change control.

stem: A certification body asks the studio to show that the test results submitted for version 3.0 last spring can be reproduced exactly. How does configuration management help?
options: It does not help: old test results cannot be reproduced
Running the test on the latest build gives the same result
It provides the defect density of version 3.0
It allows the team to revert to the earlier baseline and reproduce the previous test results
why: CM keeps baselines and their changes, so the team can go back to a previous baseline to reproduce earlier results.

distractorNotes.A: Reproducing previous results is exactly what reverting to a baseline allows.
distractorNotes.B: The test object has changed since version 3.0.
distractorNotes.C: Defect density is a metric; it does not reproduce the test.

stem: For a complex configuration item such as a test environment, what does configuration management record?
options: The items it consists of, their relationships and their versions
Only the date when it was set up
Only the people who use it
Only the defects found in it
why: For complex configuration items, CM records the parts, how they relate and their versions.

distractorNotes.B: Too little to identify or rebuild the environment.
distractorNotes.C: Users are not what CM records.
distractorNotes.D: Defects are handled in defect management.

stem: Which statement about configuration management supporting testing is CORRECT?
options: CM is only needed in sequential projects; DevOps pipelines replace it
CM covers the code, but testware is outside its scope
All configuration items, including test items, are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes and related to each other, so traceability is kept
CM is another name for defect management
why: This is what CM must ensure to support testing; documentation and software items must also be referenced unambiguously in testware.

distractorNotes.A: DevOps pipelines normally include automated CM.
distractorNotes.B: Testware is explicitly among the configuration items.
distractorNotes.D: Adjacent-concept swap: they are different processes.

stem: In a studio's CI/CD pipeline, every build is tagged automatically, and its asset bundle versions and test results are stored with it. Which statement fits?
options: This is risk monitoring
This is test completion
This is only test monitoring, not configuration management
This is automated configuration management, which a DevOps pipeline normally includes
why: CI/CD and its testing are usually part of a DevOps pipeline that includes automated configuration management.

distractorNotes.A: Risk monitoring checks mitigation and watches for new risks.
distractorNotes.B: Completion collects data at milestones; this happens on every build.
distractorNotes.C: Identifying and versioning builds and their results is CM.

stem: In a defect report, what does severity describe?
options: How often the failure occurs
The degree of impact the defect has on the interests of stakeholders or on the requirements
How urgently the defect should be fixed
How hard the defect will be to fix
why: Severity is the degree of impact of the defect.

distractorNotes.A: Frequency trap: how often it happens is not severity.
distractorNotes.C: That is priority.
distractorNotes.D: Fix effort is neither severity nor priority.

stem: A strategy game crashes to the desktop when a player opens the map during one particular cutscene, which very few players ever do. Launch is next week and the team has many more visible issues. Which rating is most appropriate?
options: High severity, low priority
Low severity, low priority, because it rarely happens
Low severity, high priority
High severity, high priority, because every crash must be fixed first
why: A crash has a high impact when it happens (high severity); because it is rare and other issues are more urgent, it can be low priority.

distractorNotes.B: Frequency trap: rarity lowers urgency, not the impact of a crash.
distractorNotes.C: A crash to desktop is not low severity.
distractorNotes.D: Overgeneralisation: priority is a business decision weighing urgency; not every crash is fixed first.

stem: The splash screen still shows a partner's old logo. Nothing else is affected, but the partner contract requires the new logo at launch, three days away. Which rating is most appropriate?
options: High severity, high priority
Low severity, low priority, because it is only cosmetic
High severity, low priority
Low severity, high priority
why: A wrong logo does not affect how the game works (low severity), but the contract deadline makes it urgent (high priority).

distractorNotes.A: The impact on the game's functions is low; urgency does not raise severity.
distractorNotes.B: Cosmetic means low severity, but the contract deadline makes it urgent.
distractorNotes.C: Neither: the impact is low and the urgency is high.

stem: Who usually decides the priority of a defect?
options: The tester who found it, alone
The developer who will fix it
The business side, for example the product owner or a triage meeting; the tester may suggest a priority
Nobody: priority is calculated automatically from severity
why: Priority is about business urgency, so it is set or confirmed by the business side, often in triage.

distractorNotes.A: Wrong actor: the tester records severity and may suggest a priority.
distractorNotes.B: Wrong actor: the developer is not the one weighing business urgency.
distractorNotes.D: Severity and priority are independent.

stem: Which statement about severity and priority is CORRECT?
options: A defect can have high severity and low priority
Priority always equals severity
A defect that affects only a few players always has low severity
A cosmetic defect can never be high priority
why: Severity (impact) and priority (urgency) are independent; all four combinations exist.

distractorNotes.B: They are independent.
distractorNotes.C: Frequency or reach does not set the impact when it occurs.
distractorNotes.D: A visible cosmetic defect (e.g. on a store page) can be very urgent.

stem: Which of these defects has the HIGHEST severity?
options: The main menu says "Contine" instead of "Continue"
When cloud sync fails, which is rare, every save file on the account is corrupted
A hat in the shop shows the wrong colour in its preview
Subtitles appear half a second late in one cutscene
why: Loss of all player data is the highest impact; rarity affects priority, not severity.

distractorNotes.A: A cosmetic defect: low impact, however visible.
distractorNotes.C: A cosmetic defect: low impact.
distractorNotes.D: A minor defect: low impact.

stem: A defect report has a title, steps to reproduce, the expected and actual results, severity and priority. A developer cannot reproduce the failure because she does not know which build or platform it happened on. Which item is missing?
options: The root cause of the defect in the code
The name of the developer responsible for the failure
Identification of the test object and the test environment
The expected result
why: A defect report should identify the test object (e.g. build) and the test environment (e.g. platform, firmware).

distractorNotes.A: Finding the root cause is debugging; a tester reports the observed failure.
distractorNotes.B: Reports are factual and neutral; blame is not a field.
distractorNotes.D: The stem says the expected result is there.

stem: A defect report reads: "Title: Shield break sound plays twice. Build 1.8.0, PS5. Steps: 1. Equip the iron shield. 2. Block a heavy attack until the shield breaks. Actual: the break sound plays twice. Severity: low. Priority: medium." Which important item is missing?
options: The severity
The steps to reproduce
The test environment
The expected result
why: Expected and actual results are both needed; without the expected result, the developer cannot be sure what correct behaviour is.

distractorNotes.A: The severity is given (low).
distractorNotes.B: The steps are given.
distractorNotes.C: The build and platform are given.

stem: Which defect report is the BEST?
options: "Lantern quest broken again after the latest build! The quest team clearly did not test their code properly. Severity: high. Please fix this as soon as possible."

"Quest 'Lost Lantern' cannot be finished after reloading a save (build 3.2.0, Switch). Steps: start the quest, save, reload, talk to the keeper. Expected: lantern in inventory. Actual: lantern missing, quest stuck. Severity: high. Recording attached."
"Several quests feel buggy after saving and loading on Switch, and the menus are slow too. Expected: everything works. Actual: it does not. Severity: medium."
"Quest 'Lost Lantern' (build 3.2.0, Switch): the problem is probably the save serializer dropping quest items on reload. Severity: high. Please check the serializer."
why: It identifies the build and platform, gives exact steps, expected and actual results, severity and evidence: enough to reproduce and resolve.

distractorNotes.A: No steps, environment or expected and actual results, and it blames people: not factual or neutral.
distractorNotes.C: Vague, with no build or steps, and it mixes several problems; one defect per report, with exact steps and results.
distractorNotes.D: A guess at the cause instead of the observed failure, with no steps or expected and actual results.

stem: Which of the following is an objective of a defect report?
options: To provide ideas for improving the development and test process
To record who is to blame for the failure
To replace the test cases that found the failure
To prove that the product is ready for release
why: Defect reports give enough information to resolve the defect, a means to track work product quality, and ideas for process improvement.

distractorNotes.B: Defect reports are not about blame.
distractorNotes.C: They reference test cases; they do not replace them.
distractorNotes.D: No report proves readiness.

stem: A tester reports that enemies stop chasing the player at the edge of a swamp. Analysis shows this is the behaviour the designers specified. What should happen to the report?
options: It is deleted, leaving no record
The developers change the behaviour anyway, because it was reported
It is classified as not being a defect and closed, for example with the status "rejected"
It stays open until the next release
why: Not every anomaly is a defect: after analysis it may be a false positive or a change request, and the report is closed accordingly (e.g. rejected).

distractorNotes.A: Reports are closed through the workflow, not erased.
distractorNotes.B: If it is the intended behaviour, a change would be a change request, not a fix.
distractorNotes.D: Leaving it open does not follow the workflow to closure.

stem: A developer has fixed a defect, and the fix is in the new build, but nobody has retested it yet. Which status should the defect report have?
options: Closed
Re-opened
Deferred
Awaiting confirmation testing
why: Once fixed, the defect waits for confirmation testing before it can be closed.

distractorNotes.A: It cannot be closed before the fix has been confirmed.
distractorNotes.B: Re-opened is for a defect whose fix failed confirmation testing or that came back.
distractorNotes.C: Deferred is for a defect whose fix has been postponed.

stem: Which information in a defect report describes the CONTEXT of the defect?
options: The test case being run, the test activity and the test data used
The expected and actual results
The severity and priority
The unique identifier and title
why: The context covers the test case, test activity, SDLC phase and other information such as the technique, checklist or test data used.

distractorNotes.B: These are their own fields in the report.
distractorNotes.C: These are their own fields in the report.
distractorNotes.D: These identify and summarise the report.

stem: A tester runs a test case on a new build and observes a failure. In which test activity is the defect report typically logged?
options: Test completion
Test execution
Test analysis
Test planning
why: Defect reports are created when failures are observed during test execution (static testing defects are handled in the same way).

distractorNotes.A: Completion collects open defects and lessons learned; the report already exists by then.
distractorNotes.C: Analysis identifies test conditions before any test is run.
distractorNotes.D: Planning comes before any test is run.
